1.pericope_label: Dinah goes out, and is defiled by Shechem

schools.summary: Calvin makes the blame partly exegetical. Moses in part casts it upon Dinah herself when he says she went out to see the daughters of the land, whereas she ought to have remained under her mother's eyes in the tent, the virtue the proverb assigns to women, that they be keepers of the house, suiting girls also; from which he warns fathers of families to keep their daughters under strict discipline, since if a vain curiosity was so heavily punished in the daughter of holy Jacob, not less danger hangs over weak virgins today. On Shechem he is milder than might be expected: having once abused her he did not treat her with contempt as men use harlots, but loved her as a wife and did not object even to circumcision to have her, though the fervour of lust had so prevailed that he first subjected her to disgrace, and in that want of self-government he grievously sinned. He finds a laudable modesty in the young man's leaving the match to his father's authority, and turns it into a weapon: since Shechem under the guidance of nature asked his father to procure his marriage, the right of parents over their children is inviolable, and this fornicator alone is judge enough to condemn the Pope for breaking that bond. Of Jacob's silence he denies that it was a deferring of vengeance; alone and devoid of counsel and consolation the man lay prostrate as one disheartened, or else was restrained by prudence from making his feelings public before he was prepared to meet the danger. Gill supposes the report reached him from one of the maids who attended her, and calls this his first affliction in his own family, though not his last.

Henry lays the disaster at the door of a girl's vain curiosity. Dinah was, so far as appears, Jacob's only daughter and therefore the mother's fondling, and those children seldom prove the best or the happiest that are most indulged. Being solitary at home with none of her own age and sex to converse with, she went out to see the daughters of the land, to see how they dressed and how they danced and what was fashionable among them, perhaps at a ball, and perhaps unknown to her father. She went to see, he adds, yet that was not all: she went to be seen too, and it may be with some thoughts of the sons of the land — the beginning of sin being as the letting forth of water. On Shechem's suit he marks the contrast with Amnon, who hated the woman he had wronged. In Jacob's silence he hears a man astonished who knows not what to say, and adds an uncomfortable possibility, that he had left the management of his affairs too much to sons who had lately grown bold and assuming, for things never go well when the authority of a parent runs low in a family.

Wesley repeats Henry's sentence about going to see and to be seen, and sets Dinah's age at fifteen or sixteen. Clarke will not have the blame divided at all. Rendering the phrase literally, that Shechem spoke to her heart, he takes it as evidence that there had been no consent on Dinah's part, that the whole was an act of violence, and that she was now detained by force in Shechem's house, where she was still found when Simeon and Levi sacked the city. He also corrects a misreading the English invites: Hamor was the prince of the country, Shechem only the prince's son.

Keil glosses the kind speech to Dinah as an attempt to comfort her with the promise of a happy marriage. Ellicott takes up the chronology, arguing from Hamor's later proposal that the people should let these men dwell in the land that Jacob was plainly a new comer, so that Dinah's dishonour took place within a few weeks of his arrival at Shechem rather than years after it. Of Jacob's silence he says it was caution, the man being no match for the Hivites, and Leah's sons having the right to uphold their sister's honour.

6.pericope_label: Hamor sues for the match, and Jacob's sons answer deceitfully

schools.summary: Calvin reports the alternative rendering against Israel and then presses the clause that follows, which is commonly given as meaning that such a thing ought not to be done; in his judgment it describes the brothers instead, who had determined with themselves that the injury was not to be borne. He thinks their indignation ought to have been mitigated by Hamor's courteousness, the old man being prince of the city while they were strangers, offering equitable conditions and pleading for his son, so that to remain implacable was a sign of most cruel pride, since they were not moved even by the prayers of one who had wronged them through blind love and without malicious intention. On the answer they gave he adds the sacramental charge: they sever the sign from the truth it represents, as if a man might pass into the Church of God merely by laying aside his uncircumcision. Gill observes that though Onkelos, Jonathan and Jarchi render the word as though the sons answered with wisdom, it is never used in a good sense, and if it was wisdom it was carnal wisdom, disapproved by plain-hearted Jacob; and he notes that in those times a man did not receive a portion with his wife but gave one, to her or to her parents for her.

Henry finds the doctrine in the name folly in Israel: uncleanness is folly, sacrificing the favour of God and peace of conscience to a brutish lust. He is uneasy about the brothers' anger even so, since they were influenced perhaps rather by jealousy for the honour of their family than by any sense of virtue, and many are concerned at the shamefulness of sin who never lay to heart the sinfulness of it. Of the treaty he makes the comment that shames the story, that in it the Canaanites were the more honest of the parties. He allows the pretence of circumcision was specious and would have been commendable if sincere, professors not being meant to marry the profane; but the Shechemites were to be circumcised not to make them holy, which was never intended, but to make them sore and so an easier prey to the sword — and bloody designs have often been carried on most securely under a pretence of religion, dissembled piety being double iniquity.

Wesley notes with Henry that folly in Israel speaks the language of after-times, Israel being not yet a people but a family only. Clarke prefers to keep the phrase contemporary by translating the preposition otherwise: not in Israel but against Israel, so that the offence is aggravated by being done against the prince of God himself, both names standing in the sentence — Jacob, whose daughter was defiled, and Israel, against whom the wrong was committed. Of the deceitful answer he says nothing could excuse it, yet notes that the parenthesis pleads provocation: they spoke so because he had defiled their sister.

Ellicott makes the same observation about the word Israel into an argument, that using it for the household as distinguished from the man belongs to the age of Moses and shows his hand in the weaving of these records. He sets out what Hamor actually proposed, that Jacob's family abandon their nomad life and settle, trading and acquiring not movable goods only but immovable property, the two clans coalescing into one community; and he separates the two marriage payments, the mohar being the price paid to the bride's kindred though it takes the form of a present, the matthan the gift made to the bride herself. Keil observes that the terms seemed reasonable to the two suitors, and that the note of Shechem's prompt compliance stands in the narrative by anticipation.

18.pericope_label: The Shechemites are persuaded and circumcised

schools.summary: Calvin is unkind to the father. He ought at the outset to have corrected his son's fault severely; instead he covers it and yields to every wish, and that an old man should for his son's sake adopt a new religion and suffer a wound in his own flesh cannot be acquitted of folly. At the gate Calvin watches the argument being chosen: it was no light thing to bring a whole people to so great a change, so Hamor and his son reason from utility, which is natural rhetoric, since honour makes the more plausible appearance but is for the most part cold in persuasion, while among the common sort utility carries almost every point. They praise Jacob's household for honesty and quiet habits, urge that the land is wide enough for both, and conceal the private and real cause of the request, so that all these pretexts were fallacious — men of rank commonly making everything serve their own ends while feigning care for the common good, so that hypocrisy appears so deeply rooted that it is a wonder to find anyone quite free of it. Let the people govern themselves too, he adds, lest they be caught by a specious show of good, as fishes are by the hook. Of their consent he grants that it looks like modesty and humanity, but holds that to change religion so carelessly betrays a gross contempt of God, since men who seriously worship do not cast aside their superstitions until convinced by sound doctrine: search the isles, says the prophet, and see whether any nation has deserted its gods, which yet are no gods. Gill divides the suitors' motive, Hamor moved by love of his son and Shechem by love of Dinah, and notes that the gate was where courts were held and city business transacted.

Henry accounts for the two suitors' compliance charitably. They were moved not only by the strong desire to bring the match about but by what they may have heard of the sacred and honourable intentions of this sign in the family of Abraham — many who know little of religion, he adds, yet know so much of it as makes them willing to join themselves with those who are religious. Of the argument that carried the town he allows the reasoning its force and condemns the principle: it was bad enough to marry on such a footing, covetousness being the greatest matchmaker in the world, and worse to be circumcised on it, since there are many with whom gain is godliness. He says shortly what the sequel will prove, that they submitted to serve a turn, to please their prince and enrich themselves, and that as nothing secures us better than true religion, so nothing exposes us more than religion only pretended to.

Wesley joins Henry in reading the suitors' motive charitably, and states the town's calculation plainly: Jacob's sons were thriving people, and an alliance promised to improve trade and bring money into the country. Clarke calls it a bait held out to the unsuspecting people by their prince and his son, who were themselves not much less deceived, and explains the town's obedience from the manners of the East, where petty princes have always been absolute and their subjects prompt and blind — the old man of the mountain answered an ambassador who required homage by bidding one attendant stab himself and another leap from the tower, then remarking that seventy thousand were thus attentive to his commands.

Ellicott infers from their readiness that circumcision must have been a rite not only well known but reckoned honourable, or they would not so easily have submitted to a thing so painful. He finds real plausibility in Hamor's case as well, since in so young a community a large accession of women was a valuable increase of strength, and guests rich in cattle would raise Shechem high among the petty states of Canaan.

25.pericope_label: Simeon and Levi destroy Shechem and spoil the city

schools.summary: Calvin will not build anything on the third day: the Hebrews think the pain was then most severe, but he judges the proof neither valid nor of much moment. On how many struck he is more definite — though Moses names two, they were leaders of a troop drawn from a large household, and the deed is ascribed to them as Carthage is said to have been destroyed by Scipio. Being Dinah's brothers by both parents, he says, they were impelled less by the reproach brought on the elect race, of which they had lately boasted, than by the infamy brought on themselves. Of the plunder he reads the phrase about coming upon the slain either of making a way over the bodies or of adding spoil to slaughter, and says that from murderers they became robbers, since he who gives himself the rein in one wickedness soon breaks out into another. Gill explains the timing from medicine: the pain of circumcision was sharpest on the third day, the part more inflamed and the man more feverish, as physicians observe of other wounds, Hippocrates having advised not to meddle with a wound on the third or fourth day lest it rankle and bring on fever. He marks the retaliation in the spoiling, and pities Shechem, who deserved better than the sword, while Hamor perhaps died for conniving at his son's sin.

Henry lays out the aggravations of the crime. It should have been considered how far Dinah was accessory: had Shechem abused her in her mother's tent it would have been another matter, but she went upon his ground and perhaps struck the spark that began the fire — when we are severe upon the sinner we ought to consider who was the tempter. Shechem had done ill, but was endeavouring to atone, and was as honourable after the deed as the case would admit. And what was his sin to all the Shechemites? Does one man offend, and must the innocent fall with the guilty? Worst of all was the treachery, since they acted as sworn enemies towards men who had just become sworn friends, making as light of their covenant as of the laws of humanity: are these the sons of Israel? Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce. He adds a fifth charge, that they made a holy ordinance serve a wicked design and so brought reproach on the badge of their religion. In the outcome he finds God's righteousness, since the men who had asked shall not their cattle be ours lost their own instead: those who unjustly grasp at what is another's justly lose what is their own.

Wesley repeats Henry's aggravations almost verbatim, and notes that the rest of the brothers, by coming on the slain, made themselves accessory to the murder. Clarke describes the state of the town: the inflammation at its height and the fever following left the sufferer helpless, so the brothers came on the city unsuspected and in no danger of resistance. He supposes the servants who helped with the flock were among them, and observes that two men could never have carried off the women, children and cattle unaided.

Ellicott guesses that Reuben and Judah, bound by the same tie of blood, were shut out of the plot, the one as feeble and opposed to bloodshed, the other as too honourable; and against Henry, who reckons the pair young men not much above twenty, he holds they must have been of ripe manhood before they could have had influence enough for so terrible an exploit. He says the two took Dinah and went out, the general plundering following after, and corrects the rendering of the last item of spoil: the word is not little ones but the household persons, the men-servants and maid-servants, who would be the most valuable part of it. Keil notes what followed at once, that Jacob reproved the originators most severely for having made him an abomination among the inhabitants of the land.

30.pericope_label: Jacob rebukes Simeon and Levi, and they answer him

schools.summary: Calvin observes that Moses records the rebuke lest anyone suppose the holy man had shared in the counsel, and that the Canaanites and Perizzites are named because, though they had suffered no wrong, they were by nature prone to inflict injury. He then raises against Jacob the objection a reader feels, asking why he is not rather angry at their cruelty, offended at their perfidy, sharp against their rapaciousness, and answers it: seeing them already terror-stricken, he probably suited his words to their state of mind, complaining as though it were he and not the Shechemites who had been killed, for men are seldom drawn to repentance except by fear of punishment, especially when they have a specious pretext to cover the fault. In the sons' two words he finds both ferocity and stupidity — barbarous, that they excuse the destruction of a whole people by the injury of one man, answer their father so contumaciously, and obstinately defend a revenge rashly taken; and senseless, that they were untouched by the prospect of their own death and their families', which seemed at hand. Intemperate anger, he concludes, deprives men of their senses, and it is not enough to lay blame on our opponents unless we also see how far it is lawful for us to go. Gill notes the pert and unseemly manner of the retort, and reports the Targums expanding it — that Shechem should not be left to boast of Dinah as of a harlot whom no man seeks to avenge — with the insinuation that Jacob had not resented the wrong as he ought.

Wesley presses Jacob's arithmetic: though he knew God had promised to preserve his house, he might justly fear that these vile practices would amount to a forfeiture and cut off the entail, for when sin is in the house there is reason to fear ruin at the door. On the retort he concedes the premise and denies the inference — no, Shechem should not have dealt so with her; but must they be their own avengers, and could nothing less than a whole city atone for the abuse? Clarke paraphrases the complaint as distress of mind and danger to the person, the deed having made Jacob odious to the surrounding tribes, who when it gets abroad will confederate against him and extirpate his family; and he settles the question of Jacob's sincerity from elsewhere, since the resentment was certainly not dissembled, Jacob having afterwards deprived these two sons of the birthright they would otherwise have enjoyed. He ends with a lexicon and a reckoning: the word for harlot occurs here first, and is not the term rendered concubine but one meaning a woman who prostitutes herself for hire; and blame attaches to all parties — to Jacob, for suffering his daughter to go out alone; to Shechem most of all, though it would be unjust not to add that he wished to make every reparation in his power, and in that is a saint beside profligates who make none and glory in their shame; and to the brothers, whose act was diabolical. Of the religious cloak thrown over it he asks how often the religion of God has been made a covert for the worst of crimes, and answers that were it not so good as it is, it could not be so abused.

Ellicott judges the rebuke inadequate. Jacob's timidity led him to think first of the danger and only afterwards of the cruelty and treachery, so that his reproof is singularly weak and the retort of his sons just — though in avenging that wrong they had committed a crime of a deeper dye.
